notes:
Verses 2, 3, 6, 7, 11, 14–15, 17–20, 25 and 30–34 aren't covered below. I couldn't read enough on them, so I left them out as you asked. The Enduring Word page wouldn't open, so David Guzik's views come from his Blue Letter Bible study guide (via search excerpts) and from quotes on Precept Austin.

## Notes on Leviticus 16

**v. 1**
- **Traditional reading:** This verse ties the chapter to Leviticus 10. The death of Aaron's sons shows why a ceremony was needed to restore fellowship between God and Israel (Richard Hess). The rules were given so other priests wouldn't die the same way. https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_16_commentary
- **Purpose of the day:** Gordon Wenham says the main aim was to cleanse the sanctuary of the pollution brought in by unclean worshippers, so that God could keep living among his people. https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_16_commentary
- **Name of the day:** Guzik notes that ancient Jews called it "the great day." It is still the only fast the Jewish calendar commands, though no sacrifice is offered today. https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_16_commentary

**v. 4: the linen garments (a real disagreement)**
- **Humility view (Wesleyan writers):**
  - Adam Clarke says it was a day of humiliation. Aaron appears before God as a sinner, so he wears humble clothes. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/16-4.html
  - Wesley: it was a day of mourning, not feasting, when people laid aside their ornaments. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/16-4.html
  - Matthew Poole gives a similar reason. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/16-4.htm
- **Purity view (Pulpit Commentary):** It rejects the humility reading, since white isn't what penitents wear. The white stands for the purity the day's rites brought about. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/16-4.htm
- **Pointing to Christ (Baptist writers):**
  - John Gill sees two things in the linen: Christ's purity, and his low estate of suffering. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/16-4.html
  - Spurgeon calls Aaron "a humbled priest" on this day. https://studylight.org/commentaries/spe/leviticus-16.html
- **Matthew Henry:** Christ atoned not in the robes of his glory but in "the linen garments of our mortality." https://studylight.org/commentaries/mhm/leviticus-16.html
- **Precept Austin:** The Greek Old Testament uses the same word for Aaron's tunic as John 19:23 uses for Jesus' garment at the cross. https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_16_commentary
- **Catholic:** The old Catholic Encyclopedia notes that Josephus says the high priest wore gold vestments. Edersheim's solution is that he wore the rich robes first and changed into linen before entering the Most Holy Place. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/12407b.htm

**vv. 5, 7–10: the two goats and the lots**
- **One offering:** Barnes says the two goats were a single sin offering. Two animals were needed to show something that had to happen after death. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/16-8.htm
- **The lots:** Barnes says casting lots left the choice to God. Gill links this to God's set plan for Christ's death. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/16-8.htm
- **Later Jewish practice:** Ellicott and Gill describe two matching tablets marked "For Jehovah" and "For Azazel." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/16-8.htm
- **Both goats picture Christ:** Benson and Poole say the slain goat pictures his death and the live goat his resurrection. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/16-8.htm
- **What "Azazel" means (disputed among commentators, not along denominational lines):**
  - *A personal evil being:* Ellicott (Anglican), Barnes and Keil-Delitzsch argue this, because "for the LORD" and "for Azazel" are set side by side. Ellicott and Barnes say the sins are sent back to the source of sin. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/16-8.htm
  - *"Complete removal":* Guzik prefers this and thinks Azazel simply describes what the goat does. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/archives/guzik_david/StudyGuide2017-Lev/Lev-16.cfm
  - *"The goat sent away":* Clarke explains it this way. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/ncv/leviticus/16-10.html Allen Ross says the word's roots point to "a goat that goes away." https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_16_commentary
  - *A mountain near Sinai:* the Geneva Study Bible notes some held this, but it prefers "scapegoat." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/16-8.htm
- **Modern scholarship:**
  - The NET Bible notes say most scholars today see Azazel as the name of a desert demon. Other options it lists are "the goat that departs" and a name for rough ground. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=lev+16%3A8-10
  - Bible Odyssey lists a place, a foreign god, or a desert demon. It says the "demon" reading rests on the Yahweh/Azazel parallel in v. 8. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/scapegoat/
- **Catholic:** The Catholic Encyclopedia says the Vulgate's "emissary goat" stands for the obscure word Azazel. It thinks the evil-spirit reading is "with better reason." https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/02054a.htm

**vv. 12–13: incense**
- Matthew Henry says the incense pictured the prayers Christ always makes for us behind the veil. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lev/Lev_016.cfm

**v. 16: atonement for the sanctuary**
- Wenham stresses that the sanctuary itself is cleansed. https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_16_commentary
- Duane Lindsey adds that the live goat's role means the people's sins were carried away in their place, which turned aside God's wrath. https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_16_commentary
- Bible Odyssey (scholarship) says the whole ritual removes built-up contamination. In its view the scapegoat carries the contamination from deliberate sins out of the tabernacle area. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/scapegoat/

**vv. 21–22: sending the goat away**
- **Laying on hands:** a standard Bible encyclopedia says this was simply a sign that guilt was passed to the goat. https://biblehub.com/topical/a/azazel.htm
- **Alexander MacLaren:** The slain goat stands for paying for sin, and the sent-away goat for its complete removal. Christ does both in one sacrifice. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/maclaren_alexander/expositions-of-holy-scripture/leviticus/scapegoat.cfm
- **GotQuestions:** Christ is our scapegoat (2 Cor 5:21; Isaiah 53:6). Like the goat driven out, he was crucified outside the city. https://www.gotquestions.org/Azazel-scapegoat.html
- **Lutheran (Indiana District of the LCMS):** Jesus is our scapegoat, carrying sins into "the deepest wilderness — the grave." The writer mentions that some see the goat as a picture of Satan, but rejects this. https://in.lcms.org/the-day-of-atonement-goats/
- **Debated teaching (Seventh-day Adventist):** GotQuestions reports that Adventist teaching makes Satan the scapegoat that bears believers' sins, citing Ellen White's *The Great Controversy*. https://www.gotquestions.org/Seventh-Day-Adventism.html GotQuestions says this contradicts 1 Peter 2:24. https://www.gotquestions.org/Ellen-G-White.html
- **Later Jewish customs:** Guzik reports a tradition that a scarlet cloth on the goat turned white if God accepted the offering. Later, the goat was pushed off a cliff. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/archives/guzik_david/StudyGuide2017-Lev/Lev-16.cfm

**vv. 23–24**
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says Aaron bathed, put his full high priest's dress back on, and offered the two rams as burnt offerings. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/16-27.htm

**vv. 26–28**
- Keil-Delitzsch says the goat's handler and those who burned the carcasses had to wash because animals loaded with sin had made them unclean. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/16-27.htm

**v. 27: burned outside the camp**
- The Pulpit Commentary says Hebrews 13:12 sees in Christ suffering "outside the camp" a sign that his blood was carried into heaven. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/16-27.htm
- John Piper (Baptist): the bodies couldn't be eaten and had to be burned outside the camp, which points to Jesus. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-sacrifice-of-praise
- MacArthur (quoted on Precept Austin) agrees it represents Christ's death outside Jerusalem. https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_16_commentary

**v. 29**
- The Catholic Encyclopedia says the law required a fast here, with work and eating banned from evening of the ninth day to evening of the tenth. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/01067a.htm
- One flag: its "Day of Atonement" article says the "nineteenth day of Tishri." https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/02054a.htm Its calendar article gives 10 Tishri, which matches the verse, so "nineteenth" looks like an error. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/03158a.htm
- Matthew Henry: the law of grieving over sin lasts until all tears are wiped away. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/16-8.htm

**v. 34: once a year**
- Matthew Henry, following Hebrews 10, says repeating the sacrifice every year showed it couldn't take sin away. Only Christ's once-for-all offering could. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/16-8.htm
- Catholic reading: these rites point to the Cross and to "the propitiatory Sacrifice which is daily renewed in a bloodless manner on the Eucharistic Altar." https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/02054a.htm

## Gaps
- **Protestant traditions:** I found no clear split along denominational lines. The real disagreements (the meaning of the linen in v. 4, the meaning of Azazel in vv. 8–10) are between individual commentators.
- **Not found:** Orthodox sources (oca.org), prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter, and Reformed teaching from ligonier.org or thegospelcoalition.org. Calvin's commentary is on biblehub, but I didn't read it.
